Blood of the New Covenant
blŭd ŭv thē nū kŭv´ē-nant
n. phrase (the blood of Christ as that which ratifies the new covenant; rendering Greek to haima mou tes kaines diathekes)
Covenant, Latin convenire, to come together; the Greek diatheke is a disposition or testament, which is why Hebrews can argue from the law of wills. A covenant in the ancient world was cut, and the cutting was in blood.

Biblical Definition

At the table: “this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mat 26:28); “This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many” (Mar 14:24); “This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you” (Luk 22:20; 1Co 11:25). The words are Moses' words at Sinai, deliberately taken up: “Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD hath made with you” (Exo 24:8), quoted in Hebrews 9:20. The new covenant itself was promised by Jeremiah: “I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jer 31:31–34).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines covenant as a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; and, in theology, the covenant of grace, in which God engages to bestow salvation on man upon the condition that man shall believe in Christ and yield obedience to the terms of the gospel.

expand to see more

COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.

2. A writing containing the terms of agreement or contract between parties.

3. In theology, the covenant of works is that implied in the commands, prohibitions, and promises of God; the covenant of redemption is the mutual agreement between the Father and Son.

4. In church affairs, a solemn agreement between the members of a church.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:28 — "For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins."

Luk 22:20 — "Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you."

Exo 24:8 — "And Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD hath made with you concerning all these words."

Heb 9:20 — "Saying, This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you."

Jer 31:31 — "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:"

1Co 11:25 — "After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me."

Modern Corruption

The cup is called a symbol of fellowship, and the Lord called it the blood of a covenant shed for the remission of sins.

expand to see more

What the Lord said over the cup was not a new metaphor but a quotation. Moses, having read the book of the covenant to the people, sprinkled them and said, Behold the blood of the covenant which the LORD hath made with you — and every man at that table had heard the sentence since childhood. Christ takes the formula, changes one word, and applies it to Himself: this is my blood of the new testament. The claim is enormous and was made quietly at supper: the covenant at Sinai is being superseded, and the ratifying blood this time is His own.

The clause most often dropped in modern communion services is the last one: for the remission of sins. Where it goes, the Supper drifts into a fellowship meal, a memorial of a good man, an expression of the congregation's togetherness — all of which are true of it and none of which is why the blood was shed. Hebrews states the principle the whole sacrificial system rested on: without shedding of blood is no remission (Heb 9:22). The cup is not primarily about the church's unity with itself; it is about a debt discharged.

The opposite corruption re-sheds the blood, offering the cup as a fresh propitiation at each celebration. Luke's own word forbids it: this cup is the new testament in my blood — the cup is the covenant document, not the payment repeated. Jeremiah's promise, which the Lord was invoking, ends with the sentence that settles it: I will remember their sin no more. A covenant whose terms include divine forgetfulness is not one that needs renewing every Sunday; it needs remembering, which is exactly what He told them to do.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek diatheke (G1242), covenant, testament; haima (G129), blood; ekcheo (G1632), to shed, pour out; aphesis (G859), remission; Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant.

expand to see more

Greek diatheke (G1242) — covenant, testament; Matthew 26:28, Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25, Hebrews 8:8, 9:15–20.

Greek aphesis (G859) — remission, forgiveness; Matthew 26:28, Hebrews 9:22, 10:18, Acts 2:38.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; Exodus 24:8, Jeremiah 31:31–33, Genesis 15:18.

Usage

"“This is my blood of the new testament” — Moses' sentence with one word changed."

"“For the remission of sins” — the clause most often dropped."

"“I will remember their sin no more” — the covenant He was invoking."
